LOL I posted this to my math sub a while back. Those are derivatives from my research, some of them. I modeled traffic, which is to say I actually did the math that is used to model traffic, collected data, and wrote the algorithms. If you have an Elsevier subscription, you could dox me pretty easily. It's okay, but against the rules to do so, at least in public. So, if you do, don't get banned.

Anyhow, traffic is fascinating. It's a chaotic system, which means that it looks like it is unpredictable, or random, until you learn the initial starting state. There are many, many things that go into traffic patterns. Even the reflectivity of lane markings impacts throughput. Even signage fonts change throughput.

Basically, I used to play with the best traffic sim known to man. It was on big iron and we didn't usually render graphics, but it's truly awesome to see. We did render graphics for demos and sales, but normal work didn't usually involve that.

I've been retired for over a decade, as I sold my business. I still get a kick out of it when I see people interested in traffic. Pedestrian traffic is even more fun, at least visually.
This is fascinating stuff indeed, and I enjoyed your comments as well.

It's easier to just say I modeled traffic, but I actually did the math and science behind it. My research that 'forwarded the art' was concerning the complexity of traffic flow when modeled from a steady state with aggregate datum weighted by impact and variability.

Basically, I helped take traffic modeling to the computer age. That's the research that earned me my PhD. Using large sets of data to predict the traffic flow was still new and was computationally expensive. I'm not a traffic engineer, I employed traffic engineers. I'm a scientist, an applied mathematician really, and this is my domain. ;-)

It really makes me smile to see people interested.

I worked with a famous fella named Dr. Lorenz, during undergrad and then in grad school, while doing my research. He was too busy and would retire so he wasn't my advisor. If you've heard of the Butterfly Effect, that's him and his Chaos Theory.

I applied those principles to traffic modeling. That which looks random is not, if you know enough about the initial starting state. Much like the fabled butterfly can start a hurricane, a stupid fucking driver can snarl traffic up and impact tens of thousands of people.

There's a limit to the resolution for predictions. You can never predict when a drunken idiot will back the wrong way down a one way street. But, you can predict that will happen with a certain level of frequency and predict what changes might lessen the event or lower the impact it has on overall traffic throughput.

Fascinating stuff indeed, and Dr. Lorenz as well! While watching the vid I could not help but wonder how variation in traffic levels and in traffic light timing would affect the flow nbrs. Are they the flow given 'ideal' conditions for each layout, or something else? Even within the expected traffic behavior -- ie. not the drunk backing down a one-way street -- the variables must be immense.

My city put a ring road in -- completed last year -- that has non-intuitive layouts at several of the exchanges. They really are a marvel and for the most part appear to work well. I am continually amazed when I see them in use. No doubt the result of work by persons such as yourself. So thanks for that! Mind you there's a choke point at one high traffic location that really makes you scratch your head.

Those all appear to be optimal. They're just throwing some optimal traffic at various interchanges and showing the results. They aren't taking into account things like time of day, local driving behaviors - and yes those vary quite a bit, average vehicle ages, length of average trip, etc... They are just basic assumptions and modeling the interchanges. They aren't really doing anything but that. We already know what to expect for any of those. They're just showing what it looks like.

The variables are numerous and they get assigned different weights. Font signage will have a lower weight than lane width, for example. They are also not taking safety into account. You have different modeling depths. We did refined and detailed predictions. We also sold software to other modeling houses. We'd eventually expand to model pedestrian traffic. I even had a lab that we could configure a small supermarket in it. We'd then get mock shoppers and observe their progression through the store. We'd do mock building layouts, etc...

I sold back in 2007 and retired. I've been retired ever since. The industry has changed quite a bit, but I still pay attention to it. These days, you can see the video talking about plugins and whatnot. Those would be proprietary plugins to let you do what I did the math to calculate, adjusted for new information. I'd go out before the changes and collect the date. We'd make our models and they'd act on them. I'd go collect the data again, and we'd see how close to the model we'd come and use that to refine our future models.

By the way, your local traffic won't fully adjust to the ring road for 18 to 24 months, on average. Some traffic patterns take more time to adjust to and some take less. Just a roundabout takes 12 to 14 months for local traffic to adjust and for full optimization (and safety) benefits to be realized. There's some variation, but those are the averages. You will be able to see this in the number of accidents on the ring road or the feeders and with congestion and throughput. They will temporarily increase and throughput will decrease at odd intervals. It'll straighten itself out as the locals learn the route.
